title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Food & Agriculture
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Five federal agencies name food and agriculture in a warning about AI-scripted access to Siemens S7 controllers
items.content_text: The NSA, CISA, FBI, Department of Energy and EPA issued a joint advisory on 19 August warning that threat actors are combining the open-source snap7 and python-snap7 automation libraries with AI-assisted scripting to build custom tools that mimic legitimate OT monitoring software. Those tools give read and write access to Siemens S7 controller memory, configuration data and ladder logic over the S7comm protocol. Food and agriculture is named among the six most-targeted sectors. Actors locate exposed or poorly segmented devices using internet scanning services, then get in through default or weakly configured credentials rather than exploiting a vulnerability. Affected lines span the S7-200, S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 including F-series safety controllers. The agencies assess current activity as reconnaissance and capability development, with read access used to prepare for later disruptive write operations.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Joint advisory AA26-231A (NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE, EPA) — corroborated by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security

items.title: Food and beverage ransomware volume is climbing, with production stoppages the recurring outcome
items.content_text: Trade reporting on the sector counts roughly 220 ransomware attacks against food and beverage organisations so far in 2026, carried out by 46 different groups, compared with 265 incidents across the whole of 2025. The most consequential recent case in the sector was the July attack on Fairlife, Coca-Cola’s dairy subsidiary, which suspended all US production after ransomware compromised critical production systems and forced manufacturing facilities offline while containment work proceeded. Separately, federal agencies have reported that since at least March an Iranian-affiliated group has disrupted the function of programmable logic controllers across multiple US critical infrastructure sectors including food processing facilities, causing operational disruption and financial loss. The pattern across both threads is the same: the sector’s just-in-time model and perishable product mean recovery time translates directly into scrapped inventory and missed delivery windows.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: BeverageDaily sector analysis, with Fairlife production stoppage reported by Food Processing and Dairy Herd
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Sector analysis published 3 Aug 2026; Fairlife incident 16 Jul 2026

items.title: CEVA Logistics breach affects European warehouses and spills customer data through its clients
items.content_text: CEVA Logistics, one of the world’s largest shipping and logistics operators, was attacked between 29 July and 1 August, with the intrusion affecting at least eight warehouses across Europe. The France-headquartered company runs more than a thousand warehouses worldwide and reported 18.3 billion dollars in revenue last year. The consequences surfaced indirectly: several companies relying on CEVA for fulfilment disclosed that their customers’ personal information had been taken, including Dutch e-commerce group Bol, department store De Bijenkorf, eyewear company Ace & Tate and football club Ajax. Food and beverage supply chains run on the same concentrated third-party logistics model for warehousing and distribution, and cold chain adds a dimension the retail victims did not face: a warehouse management outage that delays put-away or pick is a temperature-excursion and product-integrity question, not only a service-level one.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: TechCrunch, corroborated by The Record and The Register

items.title: Refrigeration controllers can be switched off while the temperature display keeps reading normal
items.content_text: Claroty’s Team82 reported vulnerabilities in industrial refrigeration controllers from Danfoss and Copeland, with both vendors publishing advisories. The finding that matters operationally is not remote code execution — it is that an attacker able to reach the controller can disable cooling while the interface continues to report a normal setpoint and normal temperature. For a food processor or cold-storage operator that inverts the assumption every cold-chain procedure rests on: that the display, the logger and the alarm agree with the physical state of the room. A silent loss of refrigeration is a product-safety and recall event long before it is a security incident, and it can run for a full shift without triggering anything. There is no reported in-the-wild exploitation; both vendors have issued fixes and guidance.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Claroty Team82 research; Danfoss and Copeland vendor advisories — reported by SecurityWeek

items.title: Dragos counts 70 food and beverage ransomware incidents in a single quarter
items.content_text: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents involving industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up 12 percent from 1,020 in the first, with manufacturing accounting for 747, construction 176, equipment manufacturing 114 and food and beverage 70. The analytical finding matters more than the count: ransomware operators do not need control system access to disrupt industrial production, because encrypting the IT systems that support the plant is regularly enough to stop the line. Extortion also continued shifting away from file encryption toward data theft. For a food processor the supporting systems are specific and unforgiving — warehouse and inventory management, label and date-code printing, lot traceability, quality and food safety records, and the systems that release product for shipment. Several of those are regulatory prerequisites for shipping at all, so an outage stops product moving even when every filler and palletiser is running normally.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Dragos Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis — via Help Net Security

items.title: Claroty finds one in five facility cyber-physical assets a single hop from internet-exposed systems
items.content_text: Team82 analysed more than 750,000 cyber-physical assets across large facilities and found nearly one in five sitting one hop from a system making outbound internet connections. Close to 90 percent of the building management systems examined communicated over insecure protocols and 40 percent ran outdated firmware, with around a third of HVAC and cooling systems one hop from an internet-exposed system. The study covers data centres, but the asset classes translate directly to a food plant: power distribution, building management, physical access control, fire protection and refrigeration. Refrigeration is the one that deserves separate attention here, because it is usually procured and maintained under a service contract with remote monitoring enabled by the contractor, sits outside the controls engineering asset register, and has a direct line to product safety rather than merely to uptime.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Claroty Team82, State of CPS Security: Data Center Exposures — reported by SecurityWeek

items.title: Citrix is telling admins to patch NetScaler now — an unauthenticated bypass on the appliance that fronts most OT remote access
items.content_text: Citrix published bulletin CTX696939 on 20 August covering two NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway flaws. The serious one, CVE-2026-19490, is an authentication bypass carrying a CVSS score of 9.3: on Gateway and AAA virtual-server configurations an unauthenticated attacker can skip the login step entirely. The second, CVE-2026-19489, is a memory overflow that can produce unpredictable behaviour or a denial of service, and only applies where SIP ALG is enabled on a Large Scale NAT group. Fixed builds are 14.1-73.32 and 13.1-63.21 or later. Citrix, Rapid7 and Finland’s national cyber authority all said they were not aware of in-the-wild exploitation at publication, while urging immediate patching — NetScaler has a long record of exploited edge flaws. In food and beverage this appliance usually arrived with a managed-services contract and now fronts remote access for line OEMs, packaging and filling vendors and the corporate ERP that schedules production. An unauthenticated bypass there reaches the engineering path into filling, packaging and refrigeration control without needing a stolen password.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Citrix security bulletin CTX696939 — reported by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News

items.title: Fire-alarm management software stores its credentials in cleartext in memory, CISA warns
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-232-01 on 20 August covering Johnson Controls Simplex Incident Manager, the software operators use to monitor and manage Simplex fire alarm panels across a property portfolio. Versions up to and including V2.01 keep user passwords and authentication tokens unencrypted in system memory while the application runs, tracked as CVE-2026-27875 and classified as CWE-316. A local attacker who already holds low-privileged access to the workstation can read those credentials out of memory and reuse them against the application and the systems it connects to. CISA lists critical manufacturing, commercial facilities, government facilities, transportation systems and energy among the affected sectors, with deployment worldwide. Johnson Controls has published remediation guidance in JCI-PSA-2026-28. Processing plants, cold stores and distribution centres run Simplex fire detection, and in food facilities the management workstation is typically a facilities or maintenance asset on the business network — shared login, physically reachable from the plant floor, and not in any OT inventory. That is the access this flaw turns into working credentials for every panel on site.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-232-01; Johnson Controls product security advisory JCI-PSA-2026-28

items.title: August ICS Patch Tuesday: maximum-severity missing authentication in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced
items.content_text: Siemens published ten advisories in the August cycle. The most serious, SSA-834709, covers a maximum-severity missing authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices allowing a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the underlying server with elevated privileges. Siemens also fixed a critical code execution vulnerability in Siveillance Video Management Servers, and high-severity flaws in Solid Edge, Simcenter Nastran, Siemens License Server, Simcenter Femap, Parasolid and Logo! Soft Comfort. Medium-severity issues were resolved in Ruggedcom devices and Desigo controllers. Schneider Electric published advisories for NetBotz 5 and PowerChute Serial Shutdown, and Phoenix Contact issued one covering multiple PLCnext firmware flaws exploitable for denial of service or malicious SQL queries. In food plants the IoT2050 and PLCnext devices commonly appear in OEE, line-monitoring and energy-metering roles retrofitted onto existing lines — installed under a continuous improvement project rather than a controls upgrade, and rarely in the patch inventory.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Siemens ProductCERT SSA-834709, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact advisories — summarised by SecurityWeek

items.title: Cisco ASA and FTD VPN zero-day exploited to reload firewalls, added to CISA KEV
items.content_text: Cisco has patched CVE-2026-20349, a flaw in the remote-access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure Firewall Threat Defense software that attackers are exploiting to force appliances offline. A specially crafted HTTP request to the vulnerable service causes an unexpected reload and a denial-of-service condition, requiring no authentication and no user interaction. Cisco’s PSIRT confirmed active exploitation in August, and CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue with a federal remediation deadline of 14 August. Hot fixes cover ASA 9.16, 9.18, 9.20, 9.22, 9.23 and 9.24 and FTD 7.0, 7.2, 7.4, 7.6, 7.7 and 10.0. For a processor the practical risk is losing remote support during a line stoppage: these appliances typically terminate OEM and integrator access to fillers, packaging machinery and refrigeration, and a night-shift breakdown with the machine builder unable to connect is an expensive extension of an ordinary fault.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Cisco security advisory and CISA KEV catalogue — reported by Help Net Security and SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Exploitation confirmed and KEV listed Aug 2026; reported 13 Aug 2026

items.title: Four more exploited flaws added to KEV on 18 August, including Windows IKE and VMware vCenter
items.content_text: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August: CVE-2026-33824 in Microsoft Internet Key Exchange, CVE-2026-55040 in Microsoft SharePoint, CVE-2026-59310 in Broadcom VMware vCenter and CVE-2026-65400 in Apple macOS. Two further additions followed on 20 August, both in TrueConf Server. For food and agriculture, vCenter is the one that changes the risk model: multi-site processors commonly run historians, MES, quality systems and virtualised HMI servers on a shared cluster, so a compromise at the hypervisor affects every plant workload at once rather than one application. IKE terminates the site-to-site tunnels linking plants, distribution centres and corporate. SharePoint is worth a second look because food safety plans, HACCP documentation and standard operating procedures are commonly stored there and treated as ordinary business content.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Added 18 Aug 2026; two further additions 20 Aug 2026

items.title: CISA publishes an advisory for flaws in Malcolm, its own free OT monitoring suite
items.content_text: Advisory ICSA-26-230-01 covers vulnerabilities in Malcolm, the network traffic analysis suite CISA distributes free for OT and ICS environments, which could allow an attacker to cause a denial-of-service condition or execute arbitrary code. Affected versions are below 26.06.1, below 26.07.0 and up to and including 26.07.1. The same day CISA published ICSA-26-230-02, covering a stack overflow in Siemens Simcenter Nastran that can lead to remote code execution if a user is tricked into running the affected binary with a malicious string; Siemens has released fixed versions. Malcolm matters disproportionately in this sector because food and agriculture is dominated by mid-size processors and cooperatives without a commercial OT monitoring budget — exactly the profile that deploys a free CISA tool, usually on a span port with visibility into the entire plant network, and almost never inside a patch process.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-230-01 and ICSA-26-230-02

items.title: AVEVA Enterprise SCADA can be pushed into executing code through tampered serialised data
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-01, published 13 August as part of a 15-advisory batch, covers a deserialisation flaw in AVEVA Enterprise SCADA. An attacker who already holds the “DNA Authority — Operator” privilege can tamper with serialised data and have it execute as code when the server deserialises it. The 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 release families are affected, along with certain Enterprise SCADA HMI versions. CISA reports no known public exploitation targeting this flaw. AVEVA’s guidance is to restrict operator rights to trusted users, disallow BLT test clients in production, and audit devices, network topology and perimeter defences; the vendor also points to KB117814 on removing the binary formatter. Process-side food and beverage plants and multi-site operations run Enterprise SCADA above the line controls, alongside iFIX and Ignition deployments. Code execution on that server puts an attacker level with the historians and alarm servers that batch records and cold-chain monitoring depend on. The operator-privilege requirement helps — provided control-room logins are individual rather than a shift password on a laminated card.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICSA-26-225-01 — corroborated by AVEVA security bulletin AVEVA-2026-005

items.title: From 11 September 2026 exploited vulnerabilities in digital products must be reported within 24 hours
items.content_text: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations take effect on 11 September 2026. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents affecting those products: an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware, a full notification within 72 hours, and a final report within 14 days of a corrective measure being available, or within a month for a severe incident. Reporting flows through a single reporting platform to the relevant national CSIRT with simultaneous availability to ENISA, and the obligations cover products already on the EU market rather than only new releases. For food and beverage the effect is mostly on the supply side. Processing, filling and packaging equipment makers selling into the EU acquire a disclosure duty, so processors buying from European OEMs should expect faster and more formal vulnerability notification from September — and should have somewhere for it to land.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: European Commission, Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations

items.title: US and Australian agencies publish guidance on isolating OT and running that way for an extended period
items.content_text: A joint publication from US and Australian agencies sets out how critical infrastructure operators should prepare to isolate vital operational technology and supporting systems from external connectivity, and to keep operating in that isolated state for an extended period rather than the few hours most continuity plans assume. It is guidance and creates no obligation. For a food processor its value is that it converts a confident claim — that the plant can keep running if corporate is compromised — into a dependency checklist. The items that break first are seldom drawn as control-system dependencies: time synchronisation, Active Directory authentication for HMI logins, licence servers for HMI and historian software, MES order release, and label and date-code printing. Given that product cannot legally ship without date coding and lot traceability, printing is frequently the binding constraint rather than anything mechanical.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Joint US–Australian OT isolation guidance — reported by SecurityWeek
